    Appendix 6: Government Ministries and Prime Ministers of Canada Since 1867

    A Ministry, the entity that exercises the practical functions of government, is determined by the tenure of its Prime Minister. It is calculated from the day the Prime Minister takes the oath of office to the day the Prime Minister resigns, dies or is dismissed. The resignation of a Prime Minister brings about the resignation of the Ministry as a whole. A Prime Minister who resigns but later returns is said to be forming a new Ministry. Since Confederation, there have been 30 Ministries. The selection of a Ministry is the Prime Minister’s responsibility, and the Governor General follows the Prime Minister’s advice in formalizing the appointments. The power to appoint a Prime Minister rests with the Governor General.

    Footnotes

    1. 1

      The government of Sir John A. Macdonald resigned on November 5, 1873, as a result of the Canadian Pacific Railway scandal. On November 7, 1873, the Liberals under Alexander Mackenzie formed a government.

    2. 2

      Sir John Abbott served as Prime Minister from the Senate.

    3. 3

      Sir Mackenzie Bowell served as Prime Minister from the Senate.

    4. 4

      Sir Charles Tupper served as Prime Minister during the dissolution period following the end of the Sixth Session of the Seventh Parliament and before the beginning of the First Session of the Eighth Parliament.

    5. 5

      On October 12, 1917, Prime Minister Sir Robert Borden formed the 10th Ministry, known as the Unionist government, which brought together Liberal-Conservative and Liberal members of Parliament who supported conscription during World War I. All ministers continuing from the Ninth Ministry and changing offices resigned by order in council, were reappointed by order in council and were sworn in to their new offices; those continuing in their old offices were not required to be either reappointed or sworn in again. Sir Robert Borden continued as Prime Minister from his original appointment in 1911. See Robert Craig Brown, Robert Laird Borden: A Biography, vol. 2 (Toronto: Macmillan, 1980), pp. 84-90, 101-10, 123-5.

    6. 6

      According to some sources like Wayne D. Madden, ed., Canadian Guide of Leadership and Electoral History, 1867-1997, (Fort McMurray: Madden, 1998), Arthur Meighen succeeded Sir Robert Borden as the leader of the Unionist Party. Shortly thereafter, the party was officially renamed the National Liberal and Conservative Party, and then, in 1922, it again became the Liberal-Conservative Party.

    7. 7

      On June 26, 1926, Prime Minister W.L. Mackenzie King requested that the Governor General dissolve Parliament and order a general election. The Governor General declined to do so and, following the resignation of Prime Minister Mackenzie King, on June 28, 1926, called upon the Leader of the Opposition, Arthur Meighen, to form a government. On June 29, 1926, Arthur Meighen formed a government. However, his government faced Parliament for only three days before being defeated in the House on July 1, 1926. The 15th Parliament was dissolved the next day and a general election was called for September 14, 1926.

    8. 8

      John Turner was not a member of Parliament or a senator when he became Prime Minister. The House did not meet during his tenure as Prime Minister.

    9. 9

      The House did not meet during Kim Campbell’s tenure as Prime Minister.

    10. 10

      Mark Carney was not a member of Parliament or a senator when he became Prime Minister. He was named Prime Minister after the prorogation of the First Session of the 44th Parliament, which was subsequently dissolved on March 23, 2025. He was elected as a member of Parliament in the April 28, 2025, general election. His Ministry continued into the 45th Parliament.
